chunk.text: The situation with Mbappé and Vinícius is complicated. You’re trying to fit multiple superstars into the same system, and naturally, issues arise. Tactics are always a reflection of the squad. Managers don’t randomly assign roles—they try to put players in their best positions.

I remember John Terry once saying that if a striker drops deep, he’ll follow him only for a short distance—not endlessly. Similarly, Mbappé dropping too deep often becomes redundant. At times, it adds no real value to the build-up.

Mbappé seems reluctant to contribute off the ball. That forces the manager to compensate elsewhere—players like Valverde end up doing extra defensive work. This is where the issue becomes structural rather than purely tactical.

Even in midfield, there are concerns. Players like Camavinga haven’t fully developed into tempo controllers like Kroos or Modrić. That ability to dictate rhythm—choosing the right pass, timing, and weight—is still missing.

We’ve discussed this all season—Mbappé’s role, Vinícius’ role, and how they coexist. The core issue is clear: Mbappé prefers playing off the left and being the focal point. But Madrid’s system requires a striker who links play and enhances teammates, like Benzema used to.
Mbappé likes to receive the ball, take on defenders, combine quickly, and attack the box from the left channel. But does he want to adapt his role to benefit others? That’s the key question.

There’s a clear pattern—even during his PSG days with Messi and Neymar, Mbappé was more of a finisher than a creator. He received chances but didn’t create as much for others. That contrasts with Vinícius, who thrives on combination play.

Another concern is how other players are being managed. For example, Valverde often creates the most impact—driving forward, breaking lines—but gets substituted early. That disrupts the team’s rhythm.
Against teams like Benfica, Valverde was again one of the main sources of threat. Yet decisions around substitutions and rotations seem inconsistent, affecting overall balance.

There’s also a question of authority. If Mbappé is always guaranteed to start regardless of form, it creates imbalance. A manager must maintain control and make decisions based on performance, not status.
In some matches, the system becomes chaotic—too many attacking players, lack of structure, and defensive instability. It feels like compromises are being made to accommodate individuals.
Even injury management raises concerns. If Mbappé is playing through pain, that’s not bravery—it’s poor decision-making. Long-term fitness should be prioritized over short-term availability.
At elite clubs, success comes from meritocracy. If a player underperforms, they should be benched—no matter how big their name is. That standard has to apply to everyone equally.
Mbappé is a world-class player, but he’s still human—he can have bad games. The manager must have the courage to make tough decisions, even if it means benching him temporarily.

Right now, it feels like other players are being sacrificed to accommodate one individual. Young talents are played out of position, and the overall structure suffers. That’s not sustainable in the long run.

text: It feels like the system is being adjusted too much to protect one player, while the rest of the squad loses balance. At the highest level, that approach is difficult to sustain.
